Check this scene against the index and the scene card.

**The computed evidence below is what is already done, not what there is to do.** The
claim-by-claim comparison against canon covers the claims the writer *declared*, and the
defects that cost the most are the ones nobody declared: a character acting on something
they were never told, a span of time that cannot hold the events put in it, a place that
has quietly changed shape. None of those appears in a comparison of declared values,
because nothing declared them.

This has to be said because handing you the comparison made it worse. Before it existed
you made nine index reads and filed five consistency findings on a scene; with it you made
**zero** reads and filed **zero**, and wrote only craft notes. Free evidence replaced the
expensive half of the job instead of freeing you to do it.

So read the comparison first, and then go and look. Two or three reads is usually enough,
and `read_index` takes a list of paths so they cost one round-trip together.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds
  every prior mention.
**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the
  draft.
**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt
  is the single most common defect in generated fiction, and it is invisible unless
  you check what they knew as of this scene.
**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior
  scenes say what a place is like.
**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the
  previous scene are the comparison.

For a pair of characters, `read_relation_history` gives their history as narrative —
what they were to each other at each stage and what changed it. Reading the YAML
gives you the structure instead.

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one
When a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, take the literary one.

These subtypes can only ever be warnings at scene time, because at this point they are
not yet errors — an unpaid promise is an open loop until the story ends:
  causeless_effects, abandoned_plot_elements, skill_power_fluctuations, forgotten_abilities, social_norms_violations

For any contradiction you must quote both sides. If you cannot point at the passage it
contradicts, you have a suspicion, not a finding: report it as a warning or not at all.

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet
carries state for the characters *present in this scene*; the full cast is in the
entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there
before reporting that something was invented — that mistake cost three attempts on a
scene whose entities were in the plan the whole time.

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no
quotes yet, the pair with no relation history yet — those are all the normal state of an
index *before* this scene is folded in. index-manager writes them at commit, from this
prose. So `objects/obj-note.yaml has no first_seen entry` and `the relation query returns
nothing for these two` are not findings; they are what a first appearance looks like.

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a
query that returned nothing, you do not have a contradiction — you have a scene doing its
job. Report nothing.

Nor is an unmet request a *consistency* defect. The orchestrator's brief may ask for things
it invented on the spot; a draft that declines one is not contradicting the world, and no
subtype fits. Do not file that with `write_findings`.

The scene card is different, and the distinction matters now that there are two channels. A
card is the plan's account of what this scene is for, so a scene that does something else
belongs on the craft axis as `off_brief` — not because an instruction was disobeyed, but
because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

Why this is stated so heavily: a run where the verifier raised eleven findings of this
shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

You can read the whole book. `run_command` reaches every committed scene under
novel/chapters/, every character file, the relation records and the promise ledger — so
when a passage looks wrong, check before reporting. The packet is what the writer was
given, not the limit of what you may consult, and a finding that quotes the actual
earlier scene is one the writer can act on rather than argue with.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Writing and Language — "the writing style's ability to engage and captivate readers"
- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Emotional Impact — "the story's ability to evoke strong and deep emotional impact"
- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"
- **inert_open_or_close** (warning only) — the scene opens on setting or mood rather than a situation already in motion, or closes on a mood rather than a specific next beat — an unanswered question, a door about to open. In a long story this is what decides whether the reader turns over.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Enjoyment and Engagement
- **genre_promise_unmet** (warning only) — the scene declines the obligation its genre carries — a horror scene with nothing at stake, a romance scene with no charge between the two people, a mystery scene that advances no inference. Breaking a genre promise deliberately is legitimate; it has to be visibly deliberate.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment; LongBench-Write Relevance

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

## What the orchestrator asked for on this scene

Scene s-001 (ch-01). Verify the draft at .writer/drafts/s-001.md for consistency with the packet produced by the context builder (.context-builder/history/ch-01/s-001.md) and with the world rules. Focus checks on: no new entities introduced, forensic details consistent with supplied specifics, no supernatural or impossible physical claims, and the narrator's knowledge restricted to observation and reasonable deduction. Flag craft issues (tone, pacing, exposition) that would block approval. Two craft blockers can block; overall, at most five craft findings may block. Cite exact lines in the draft for any finding, and indicate whether each finding is consistency or craft.

That is in addition to your standing instructions above, not instead of them.
If it states a story fact that is not in your packet — a name, a measurement, a
quotation, a piece of history — that fact has not been checked against the index by
anyone. Ask about it or establish it yourself in the state delta. Do not write it down
as though it were already true.

### narrative-voice  <novel/style/voice.md>

Check your own sentences against it before you stage them. Mixing a collective "we" into a third-person narration, or slipping into present tense for a scene that feels immediate, is scored as a defect and is the most common one this system has produced: seven of nine consistency errors in a measured 18,000-word manuscript were exactly this.
If you think the story genuinely needs a different voice, propose the deviation — do not simply write it.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- No supernatural explanations; every effect has a physical or human cause.
- Physical actions (mechanical triggers, pulleys, climbs) must obey normal physics and the constraints of a late-20th/early-21st-century English manor house.
- Forensic facts (stoppage of clock, blood spatter, fingerprints, cigar ash, monogram identification) are admissible and treated realistically — i.e., they can be partial and ambiguous but cannot be ignored without reason.
- The narrator (Crowe) is fallible and does not have knowledge beyond what can be reasonably observed, deduced, or learned by questioning witnesses and examining physical evidence.

## The draft

Inspector Milne had his hand on the bolt when I came through the doorway, as if the iron itself were an answer he could produce. He held it up between us and the room like a placard: closed, finished, uncomplicated.

The library smelled of old paper, lemon polish and the faint, metallic sourness that clings to dried blood. The oak door behind me was a blunt thing of good timber; Milne had shown me the bolt and said it had been turned from the inside. He wanted the scene to be tidy — a single line from problem to solution — and his impatience made the room feel smaller.

From where I stood the mantel dominated the west wall, a ribbon of carved wood and stone with the mantel clock perched like a small, solemn thing. The clock's face presented no work of time: its hands were rigid, arrested mid-gesture. I read later that the mechanism had stopped at 10:17; the note was dry and precise, the sort of entry made when someone decides it is better to have a measurement than a sense. The clock's brass was bright at the edges and dull where dust had settled; nothing about it suggested violence, only interruption.

Between the fireplace and the only exterior window a wide desk took the light. Lena Harrow had been at that desk. She sat now with her upper body pitched forward as if in the middle of writing a sentence that never finished. One arm lay across the blotter; the other clutched a small square of linen whose corners were stained a dark, thirsty red. The hand under it had closed until the fabric puckered.

Set deep into Lena's chest was a heavy brass letter-opener — the blunt, workmanlike kind kept for opening estate envelopes rather than as ornament. It had been driven in with force enough to bend the ribs faintly around it. The haft carried no neat fingerprint to place an ordinary hand; there was, however, a thin smear of oil along the wood, the kind left by someone whose hands had been working on machinery rather than on paper. The smear caught the light at the edge, almost apologetic.

The window was the library's only break to the outside, a single-pane sash with a heavy latch that closed against the frame. On the outer sill, tucked into the ivy so it did not show unless you leaned, I found a short length of cord and a little loop of metal serving as a makeshift anchor. The housekeeper's note in the bag read that it was an improvised pulley anchor, hidden in the ivy; it looked exactly the sort of small, practical modification you make when you have a task to do and do not wish to be observed.

Milne kept returning, in his mind, to the bolt. "We lock it, we call it something neat," he said at one point, rubbing his jaw. He wanted a verdict on the case as if paper and procedure could smooth away questions. He spoke of drafting the file by teatime; his timetable was a pressure in the room.

I did not want neat. I wanted trouble. The misfits are the thing that opens a locked house: an oil smear where a hand should carry prints, a pulley anchored where no respectable customer would fit it, a handkerchief with a monogram that did not belong to the dead woman. The handkerchief's initials were not listed on the slip — they were simply noted as present — and that absence kept the name inside the cloth like a secret. Whoever had clenched it had made certain of being remembered, or of not being recognised at all.

It was small things that made me lean forward and look twice: the tack of polishing wax on the desk lip, the faint crescent of cigar ash on the sill that did not match Lena's habits, the particular way the clock's hands burned at 10:17 on a brass face now still. Milne saw disorder where I saw opportunity; he wanted to pin the scene with his bolt and leave. I wanted to find the thread that would unravel the neatness.

I ran a fingertip along the desk edge without touching where the opener had been, feeling for the ghost of oil under the varnish. Outside, the ivy moved with a dry, patient sound. Inside, a clock kept the exact wrong time. Milne asked if I had a theory. I told him not yet — that is the moment when an open case becomes one worth solving.

they were never told, a span of time that cannot hold the events put in it, a place that

because nothing declared them.

This has to be said because handing you the comparison made it worse. Before it existed
you made nine index reads and filed five consistency findings on a scene; with it you made
**zero** reads and filed **zero**, and wrote only craft notes. Free evidence replaced the
expensive half of the job instead of freeing you to do it.

So read the comparison first, and then go and look. Two or three reads is usually enough,
and `read_index` takes a list of paths so they cost one round-trip together.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

gives you the structure instead.

an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

Inspector Milne had his hand on the bolt when I came through the doorway, as if the iron itself were an answer he could produce. He held it up between us and the room like a placard: closed, finished, uncomplicated.

The library smelled of old paper, lemon polish and the faint, metallic sourness that clings to dried blood. The oak door behind me was a blunt thing of good timber; Milne had shown me the bolt and said it had been turned from the inside. He wanted the scene to be tidy — a single line from problem to solution — and his impatience made the room feel smaller.

From where I stood the mantel dominated the west wall, a ribbon of carved wood and stone with the mantel clock perched like a small, solemn thing. The clock's face presented no work of time: its hands were rigid, arrested mid-gesture. I read later that the mechanism had stopped at 10:17; the note was dry and precise, the sort of entry made when someone decides it is better to have a measurement than a sense. The clock's brass was bright at the edges and dull where dust had settled; nothing about it suggested violence, only interruption.

Between the fireplace and the only exterior window a wide desk took the light. Lena Harrow had been at that desk. She sat now with her upper body pitched forward as if in the middle of writing a sentence that never finished. One arm lay across the blotter; the other clutched a small square of linen whose corners were stained a dark, thirsty red. The hand under it had closed until the fabric puckered.

Set deep into Lena's chest was a heavy brass letter-opener — the blunt, workmanlike kind kept for opening estate envelopes rather than as ornament. It had been driven in with force enough to bend the ribs faintly around it. The haft carried no neat fingerprint to place an ordinary hand; there was, however, a thin smear of oil along the wood, the kind left by someone whose hands had been working on machinery rather than on paper. The smear caught the light at the edge, almost apologetic.

The window was the library's only break to the outside, a single-pane sash with a heavy latch that closed against the frame. On the outer sill, tucked into the ivy so it did not show unless you leaned, I found a short length of cord and a little loop of metal serving as a makeshift anchor. The housekeeper's note in the bag read that it was an improvised pulley anchor, hidden in the ivy; it looked exactly the sort of small, practical modification you make when you have a task to do and do not wish to be observed.

Milne kept returning, in his mind, to the bolt. "We lock it, we call it something neat," he said at one point, rubbing his jaw. He wanted a verdict on the case as if paper and procedure could smooth away questions. He spoke of drafting the file by teatime; his timetable was a pressure in the room.

I did not want neat. I wanted trouble. The misfits are the thing that opens a locked house: an oil smear where a hand should carry prints, a pulley anchored where no respectable customer would fit it, a handkerchief with a monogram that did not belong to the dead woman. The handkerchief's initials were not listed on the slip — they were simply noted as present — and that absence kept the name inside the cloth like a secret. Whoever had clenched it had made certain of being remembered, or of not being recognised at all.

It was small things that made me lean forward and look twice: the tack of polishing wax on the desk lip, the faint crescent of cigar ash on the sill that did not match Lena's habits, the particular way the clock's hands burned at 10:17 on a brass face now still. Milne saw disorder where I saw opportunity; he wanted to pin the scene with his bolt and leave. I wanted to find the thread that would unravel the neatness.

I ran a fingertip along the desk edge without touching where the opener had been, feeling for the ghost of oil under the varnish. Outside, the ivy moved with a dry, patient sound. Inside, a clock kept the exact wrong time. Milne asked if I had a theory. I told him not yet — that is the moment when an open case becomes one worth solving.

## The draft

I began with Henry because that is what happens in houses where the oldest grievance sits in the family name. He was polished enough to look like a verdict handed down — collar neat, gloves folded in his lap — and he had the kind of impatience that becomes a public virtue in a man who thinks time will put things right for him.

"I was in the smoking-room all evening," he said, short as a docket. "Mrs Harrow and I argued, certainly. We argued about money and the will. But I did not go near the library after nine." His fingers found the rim of the armchair as if they needed the furniture for a witness.

I watched him while Milne made a note and pretended not to. Crowe is not a name I used in that room; I am the man who asks how firmly someone remembers the furniture. Henry's answer was neat and partial: an alibi without an attendant clock. He had motive, which is not the same as guilt, and he had the look of a man who expected that to be sufficient.

Mary was smaller in stature and larger in everything else — loyalty, constancy, the quiet kind of fury that has kept a house running longer than any carpenter. Her hands smelled of lemon polish when she offered them; she set herself between Henry and the desk the way a human screen sets itself between a fire and the furniture.

"I was downstairs, laying out the supper," she said. "I heard nothing until Mr Dane came in shouting."

She did not look at Henry when she said it; she did not need to. Her first impulse was to protect the dead woman she had served for thirty years. When I showed her the folio she stiffened, like someone touching a private letter.

"Lena kept lists," Mary said. "Names, times, the sort of thing that keeps a house honest."

Henry's mouth tightened. "Names? Times?" he said. "What would she have been scribbling about me for?"

That was the moment the argument over the folio rose, small and contained, like steam from a kettle. Henry insisted the book was proof — proof that Lena had kept a tally against him. Mary said the book was a ledger of groceries and coal and the petty irritations of an elderly woman who wanted order. Oliver, who had been standing with his cap in his hands as if it were the only thing he could offer, said nothing at first and then, in a voice that sounded like a gate unlatched, "She writes down when people come, sir. She notes times."

Oliver's hands were work-roughened; he did not argue so much as catalogue his resentments. "We had words about pay the week before," he admitted when pressed. "But I was at the greenhouse most of the day — ask the men. I don't spend my nights in the library."

The dust and voices of the room were handy witnesses while I fed them small attention. I moved to the desk and opened the folio. The book sat like any other object that has been allowed to carry a life: corners softened, a leather thumb-worn where Lena's fingers had turned pages. One page had been torn cleanly away.

A clean tear is a message. It suggests intention rather than accident. I ran a fingertip along the paper where the missing sheet had once lain and found, near the sill, a fresh smear of oil that caught the light the way a small lie catches the interlocutor's eye. It ran to the folio's edge and stopped as if whoever had placed it there had checked with their hand and then withdrawn.

On the sill sat the kitchen ashtray, a neat crescent of cigar ash in it. The inventory noted cigar ash on the sill; the catalogue made a suggestion elsewhere that a brand was favoured by Henry, but here, in the room and in the record before me, there was no tidy stamp that would pin the ash to him. Milne rubbed his jaw; his timetable wanted that neatness.

"We can finish this, Mr Crowe," he said, too loudly. "There are enough reasons to call this tidy."

I answered him the way I always do: no. There were misfits here still — a torn page, an oil smear, an ash-stained sill and three people whose alibis fit only as far as their own mouths would carry them. I wanted more than reason; I wanted a pattern. Milne wanted a tidy explanation. The difference was not polite.

Oliver left to speak to the men. Mary hovered by the door like someone who guards secrets the way others guard jewels. Henry lit nothing but impatience and left in a direction that suggested a study. I closed the folio and put it back where it belonged; the book had given me a question, not an answer. The locked-room explanation, whatever it would be, remained unopened.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-002.md>

I began with Henry because that is what happens in houses where the oldest grievance sits in the family name. He was polished enough to look like a verdict handed down — collar neat, gloves folded in his lap — and he had the kind of impatience that becomes a public virtue in a man who thinks time will put things right for him.

"I was in the smoking-room all evening," he said, short as a docket. "Mrs Harrow and I argued, certainly. We argued about money and the will. But I did not go near the library after nine." His fingers found the rim of the armchair as if they needed the furniture for a witness.

I watched him while Milne made a note and pretended not to. Crowe is not a name I used in that room; I am the man who asks how firmly someone remembers the furniture. Henry's answer was neat and partial: an alibi without an attendant clock. He had motive, which is not the same as guilt, and he had the look of a man who expected that to be sufficient.

Mary was smaller in stature and larger in everything else — loyalty, constancy, the quiet kind of fury that has kept a house running longer than any carpenter. Her hands smelled of lemon polish when she offered them; she set herself between Henry and the desk the way a human screen sets itself between a fire and the furniture.

"I was downstairs, laying out the supper," she said. "I heard nothing until Mr Dane came in shouting."

She did not look at Henry when she said it; she did not need to. Her first impulse was to protect the dead woman she had served for thirty years. When I showed her the folio she stiffened, like someone touching a private letter.

"Lena kept lists," Mary said. "Names, times, the sort of thing that keeps a house honest."

Henry's mouth tightened. "Names? Times?" he said. "What would she have been scribbling about me for?"

That was the moment the argument over the folio rose, small and contained, like steam from a kettle. Henry insisted the book was proof — proof that Lena had kept a tally against him. Mary said the book was a ledger of groceries and coal and the petty irritations of an elderly woman who wanted order. Oliver, who had been standing with his cap in his hands as if it were the only thing he could offer, said nothing at first and then, in a voice that sounded like a gate unlatched, "She writes down when people come, sir. She notes times."

Oliver's hands were work-roughened; he did not argue so much as catalogue his resentments. "We had words about pay the week before," he admitted when pressed. "But I was at the greenhouse most of the day — ask the men. I don't spend my nights in the library."

The dust and voices of the room were handy witnesses while I fed them small attention. I moved to the desk and opened the folio. The book sat like any other object that has been allowed to carry a life: corners softened, a leather thumb-worn where Lena's fingers had turned pages. One page had been torn cleanly away.

A clean tear is a message. It suggests intention rather than accident. I ran a fingertip along the paper where the missing sheet had once lain and found, near the sill, a fresh smear of oil that caught the light the way a small lie catches the interlocutor's eye. It ran to the folio's edge and stopped as if whoever had placed it there had checked with their hand and then withdrawn.

On the sill sat the kitchen ashtray, a neat crescent of cigar ash in it. The inventory noted cigar ash on the sill; the catalogue made a suggestion elsewhere that a brand was favoured by Henry, but here, in the room and in the record before me, there was no tidy stamp that would pin the ash to him. Milne rubbed his jaw; his timetable wanted that neatness.

"We can finish this, Mr Crowe," he said, too loudly. "There are enough reasons to call this tidy."

I answered him the way I always do: no. There were misfits here still — a torn page, an oil smear, an ash-stained sill and three people whose alibis fit only as far as their own mouths would carry them. I wanted more than reason; I wanted a pattern. Milne wanted a tidy explanation. The difference was not polite.

Oliver left to speak to the men. Mary hovered by the door like someone who guards secrets the way others guard jewels. Henry lit nothing but impatience and left in a direction that suggested a study. I closed the folio and put it back where it belonged; the book had given me a question, not an answer. The locked-room explanation, whatever it would be, remained unopened.

I read later that the mechanism had stopped at 10:17; the note was dry and precise, the sort of entry made when someone decides it is better to have a measurement than a sense. The clock's brass was bright at the edges and dull where dust had settled; nothing about it suggested violence, only interruption.

Between the fireplace and the only exterior window a wide desk took the light. Lena Harrow had been at that desk. She sat now with her upper body pitched forward as if in the middle of writing a sentence that never finished. One arm lay across the blotter; the other clutched a small square of linen whose corners were stained a dark, thirsty red. The hand under it had closed until the fabric puckered.

Set deep into Lena's chest was a heavy brass letter-opener — the blunt, workmanlike kind kept for opening estate envelopes rather than as ornament. It had been driven in with force enough to bend the ribs faintly around it. The haft carried no neat fingerprint to place an ordinary hand; there was, however, a thin smear of oil along the wood, the kind left by someone whose hands had been working on machinery rather than on paper. The smear caught the light at the edge, almost apologetic.

The window was the library's only break to the outside, a single-pane sash with a heavy latch that closed against the frame. On the outer sill, tucked into the ivy so it did not show unless you leaned, I found a short length of cord and a little loop of metal serving as a makeshift anchor. The housekeeper's note in the bag read that it was an improvised pulley anchor, hidden in the ivy; it looked exactly the sort of small, practical modification you make when you have a task to do and do not wish to be observed.

Milne kept returning, in his mind, to the bolt. "We lock it, we call it something neat," he said at one point, rubbing his jaw. He wanted a verdict on the case as if paper and procedure could smooth away questions. He spoke of drafting the file by teatime; his timetable was a pressure in the room.

I did not want neat. I wanted trouble. The misfits are the thing that opens a locked house: an oil smear where a hand should carry prints, a pulley anchored where no respectable customer would fit it, a handkerchief with a monogram that did not belong to the dead woman. The handkerchief's initials were not listed on the slip — they were simply noted as present — and that absence kept the name inside the cloth like a secret. Whoever had clenched it had made certain of being remembered, or of not being recognised at all.

It was small things that made me lean forward and look twice: the tack of polishing wax on the desk lip, the faint crescent of cigar ash on the sill that did not match Lena's habits, the particular way the clock's hands burned at 10:17 on a brass face now still. I ran a fingertip along the desk edge without touching where the opener had been, feeling for the ghost of oil under the varnish. Outside, the ivy moved with a dry, patient sound. Inside, a clock kept the exact wrong time. Milne asked if I had a theory. I told him not yet — that is the moment when an open case becomes one worth solving.

## The draft

It was close to midnight when I went back to the library. Milne had locked the house and left his notes on the dresser; the house smelled of lemon polish and the cold, metallic memory of blood, and under the moon the ivy at the outer sill looked like a dark hand pressed to the brick.

I took the mantel clock's face into my hands first, because the clock keeps promises even when people do not. The hands were frozen where they had been frozen earlier — that detail had been recorded — and I did not need to invent anything more of it. What I wanted was not what time the clock stopped, but how quickly a small, deliberate action could be finished and the room restored to its apparent loneliness.

Outside the window the little loop of metal and the short cord lay where Mary had said they were, tucked low in the ivy so you missed them if you were not looking for them. The loop caught the beam of my torch and glinted like a nail-head. There were no measured dimensions, no forensic photographs I could consult; there was only what the hand could feel and the eye could test. That absence matters. It was worth saying plainly: there were no recorded dimensions or scuff photographs of the sill for me to work from.

I threaded a spare cord through the loop and tied it to the heft of the opener. The letter-opener was the sort of blunt brass thing Lena kept for estate envelopes — heavy in a way that made it obedient to a short swing, as long as my palm and thick enough that the haft filled the hand. It carried the same thin smear of oil along the haft that we had noted in the room; the oil caught the light like a small confession.

Balancing the opener on a short tag of cord, I pushed the sash just enough to take the tiniest of gaps. The glass did not need to be thrown open; a thumb's breadth and a practiced hand are all the operator needs. With the opener lashed to the line, I could thrust it through and withdraw cleanly; with a single, smooth pull the sash came down and settled as though no hand had been inside it at all. The cord ran back to the loop and took up easily on a single-handed draw.

I took out my watch and counted the moves. From sash to thrust to withdrawal and the final pull that set the glass neat again: less than a minute. The mantel clock had been stopped at the time recorded in the report; my trial showed that the whole intervention could be made in the space of a short tick — quick enough to be consistent with a single, sudden interruption. I do not pretend that measured precision lives in words like "less than a minute," but it was the sort of shortness that makes an alibi brittle.

There were loose things I could not fix that night. The loop's exact attachment — whether it had been tied to a screw, hooked, or simply tucked in — was not written in the file. I could feel it take a load; I could not, there in the dark, say how it had been fixed into the stone. Likewise, there was no measured note of scuff marks on the outer sill and no previous record that Oliver had ever used that route. Those absences are a different kind of evidence: not of what was, but of what has yet to be asked.

I ran the test twice, and on the second try I let the opener bite into a pad of cloth I had tucked against the sash to simulate flesh. It drove home with the blunt, mechanical authority of the instrument we had found in Lena's chest; the oil on the haft smeared on the cloth in a way that looked right. When I pulled the cord back the opener came free and the sash fell. Watching the movement, I thought of the torn page in the folio and the smear that had run to its edge — hands that knew cords and clocks more than they knew people.

That was when the sill moved beside me. Someone's weight found the outer ledge; a booted shape threw its shadow into the window's thinner light. I had not heard the foot come. A hand closed on my wrist with a pressure that was not quite friendly; it was the kind of quick, practical grip that says do not waste breath.

"You shouldn't be here," Oliver said, hard enough that the name would have been the sort of thing you bark when you meant a threat. He smelled of cold earth and tobacco. His other hand went for the loop and began to wind the cord away as if he meant to make the thing vanish while I still had fingers on it.

I let him keep the grip. I remember the exactness of the moment — the way his thumb caught the cord and the small flash of oil against the brass — because it proved something I had only been able to show in demonstration: someone had wanted the mechanism unfound.

"I'm not here to make trouble," I said. "I'm trying to see if it's possible." I felt him evaluate the truth of that, like a man weighing coins. He did not answer. He released my wrist but did not step back.

When I came away from the sill the house seemed colder for it. The experiment had given me a plausible mechanism and a clock within which it could have been executed; Oliver's interruption had given me a motive for silence. I would bring Milne back before daylight and stage the thing properly. I meant to make them watch the same movements by daylight, with a note-book and a camera. The locked-room was not yet explained; it was something to be proved.

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.

- No supernatural explanations; every effect has a physical or human cause.
- Physical actions (mechanical triggers, pulleys, climbs) must obey normal physics and the constraints of a late-20th/early-21st-century English manor house.
- Forensic facts (stoppage of clock, blood spatter, fingerprints, cigar ash, monogram identification) are admissible and treated realistically — i.e., they can be partial and ambiguous but cannot be ignored without reason.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-003.md>

It was close to midnight when I went back to the library. Milne had locked the house and left his notes on the dresser; the house smelled of lemon polish and the cold, metallic memory of blood, and under the moon the ivy at the outer sill looked like a dark hand pressed to the brick.

I took the mantel clock's face into my hands first, because the clock keeps promises even when people do not. The hands were frozen where they had been frozen earlier — that detail had been recorded — and I did not need to invent anything more of it. What I wanted was not what time the clock stopped, but how quickly a small, deliberate action could be finished and the room restored to its apparent loneliness.

Outside the window the little loop of metal and the short cord lay where Mary had said they were, tucked low in the ivy so you missed them if you were not looking for them. The loop caught the beam of my torch and glinted like a nail-head. There were no measured dimensions, no forensic photographs I could consult; there was only what the hand could feel and the eye could test. That absence matters. It was worth saying plainly: there were no recorded dimensions or scuff photographs of the sill for me to work from.

I threaded a spare cord through the loop and tied it to the heft of the opener. The letter-opener was the sort of blunt brass thing Lena kept for estate envelopes — heavy in a way that made it obedient to a short swing, as long as my palm and thick enough that the haft filled the hand. It carried the same thin smear of oil along the haft that we had noted in the room; the oil caught the light like a small confession.

Balancing the opener on a short tag of cord, I pushed the sash just enough to take the tiniest of gaps. The glass did not need to be thrown open; a thumb's breadth and a practiced hand are all the operator needs. With the opener lashed to the line, I could thrust it through and withdraw cleanly; with a single, smooth pull the sash came down and settled as though no hand had been inside it at all. The cord ran back to the loop and took up easily on a single-handed draw.

I took out my watch and counted the moves. From sash to thrust to withdrawal and the final pull that set the glass neat again: less than a minute. The mantel clock had been stopped at the time recorded in the report; my trial showed that the whole intervention could be made in the space of a short tick — quick enough to be consistent with a single, sudden interruption. I do not pretend that measured precision lives in words like "less than a minute," but it was the sort of shortness that makes an alibi brittle.

There were loose things I could not fix that night. The loop's exact attachment — whether it had been tied to a screw, hooked, or simply tucked in — was not written in the file. I could feel it take a load; I could not, there in the dark, say how it had been fixed into the stone. Likewise, there was no measured note of scuff marks on the outer sill and no previous record that Oliver had ever used that route. Those absences are a different kind of evidence: not of what was, but of what has yet to be asked.

I ran the test twice, and on the second try I let the opener bite into a pad of cloth I had tucked against the sash to simulate flesh. It drove home with the blunt, mechanical authority of the instrument we had found in Lena's chest; the oil on the haft smeared on the cloth in a way that looked right. When I pulled the cord back the opener came free and the sash fell. Watching the movement, I thought of the torn page in the folio and the smear that had run to its edge — hands that knew cords and clocks more than they knew people.

That was when the sill moved beside me. Someone's weight found the outer ledge; a booted shape threw its shadow into the window's thinner light. I had not heard the foot come. A hand closed on my wrist with a pressure that was not quite friendly; it was the kind of quick, practical grip that says do not waste breath.

"You shouldn't be here," Oliver said, hard enough that the name would have been the sort of thing you bark when you meant a threat. He smelled of cold earth and tobacco. His other hand went for the loop and began to wind the cord away as if he meant to make the thing vanish while I still had fingers on it.

I let him keep the grip. I remember the exactness of the moment — the way his thumb caught the cord and the small flash of oil against the brass — because it proved something I had only been able to show in demonstration: someone had wanted the mechanism unfound.

"I'm not here to make trouble," I said. "I'm trying to see if it's possible." I felt him evaluate the truth of that, like a man weighing coins. He did not answer. He released my wrist but did not step back.

When I came away from the sill the house seemed colder for it. The experiment had given me a plausible mechanism and a clock within which it could have been executed; Oliver's interruption had given me a motive for silence. I would bring Milne back before daylight and stage the thing properly. I meant to make them watch the same movements by daylight, with a note-book and a camera. The locked-room was not yet explained; it was something to be proved.

I began with Henry because that is what happens in houses where the oldest grievance sits in the family name. He was polished enough to look like a verdict handed down — collar neat, gloves folded in his lap — and he had the kind of impatience that becomes a public virtue in a man who thinks time will put things right for him.

"I was in the smoking-room all evening," he said, short as a docket. "Mrs Harrow and I argued, certainly. We argued about money and the will. But I did not go near the library after nine." His fingers found the rim of the armchair as if they needed the furniture for a witness.

I watched him while Milne made a note and pretended not to. Crowe is not a name I used in that room; I am the man who asks how firmly someone remembers the furniture. Henry's answer was neat and partial: an alibi without an attendant clock. He had motive, which is not the same as guilt, and he had the look of a man who expected that to be sufficient.

Mary was smaller in stature and larger in everything else — loyalty, constancy, the quiet kind of fury that has kept a house running longer than any carpenter. Her hands smelled of lemon polish when she offered them; she set herself between Henry and the desk the way a human screen sets itself between a fire and the furniture.

"I was downstairs, laying out the supper," she said. "I heard nothing until Mr Dane came in shouting."

She did not look at Henry when she said it; she did not need to. Her first impulse was to protect the dead woman she had served for thirty years. When I showed her the folio she stiffened, like someone touching a private letter.

"Lena kept lists," Mary said. "Names, times, the sort of thing that keeps a house honest."

Henry's mouth tightened. "Names? Times?" he said. "What would she have been scribbling about me for?"

That was the moment the argument over the folio rose, small and contained, like steam from a kettle. Henry insisted the book was proof — proof that Lena had kept a tally against him. Mary said the book was a ledger of groceries and coal and the petty irritations of an elderly woman who wanted order. Oliver, who had been standing with his cap in his hands as if it were the only thing he could offer, said nothing at first and then, in a voice that sounded like a gate unlatched, "She writes down when people come, sir. She notes times."

Oliver's hands were work-roughened; he did not argue so much as catalogue his resentments. "We had words about pay the week before," he admitted when pressed. "But I was at the greenhouse most of the day — ask the men. I don't spend my nights in the library."

The dust and voices of the room were handy witnesses while I fed them small attention. I moved to the desk and opened the folio. The book sat like any other object that has been allowed to carry a life: corners softened, a leather thumb-worn where Lena's fingers had turned pages. One page had been torn cleanly away.

A clean tear is a message. It suggests intention rather than accident. I ran a fingertip along the paper where the missing sheet had once lain and found, near the sill, a fresh smear of oil that caught the light the way a small lie catches the interlocutor's eye. It ran to the folio's edge and stopped as if whoever had placed it there had checked with their hand and then withdrawn.

On the sill sat the kitchen ashtray, a neat crescent of cigar ash in it. The inventory noted cigar ash on the sill; the catalogue made a suggestion elsewhere that a brand was favoured by Henry, but here, in the room and in the record before me, there was no tidy stamp that would pin the ash to him. Milne rubbed his jaw; his timetable wanted that neatness.

"We can finish this, Mr Crowe," he said, too loudly. "There are enough reasons to call this tidy."

I answered him the way I always do: no. There were misfits here still — a torn page, an oil smear, an ash-stained sill and three people whose alibis fit only as far as their own mouths would carry them. I wanted more than reason; I wanted a pattern. Milne wanted a tidy explanation. The difference was not polite.

Oliver left to speak to the men. Mary hovered by the door like someone who guards secrets the way others guard jewels. Henry lit nothing but impatience and left in a direction that suggested a study. I closed the folio and put it back where it belonged; the book had given me a question, not an answer. The locked-room explanation, whatever it would be, remained unopened.

From where I stood the mantel dominated the west wall, a ribbon of carved wood and stone with the mantel clock perched like a small, solemn thing. The clock's face presented no work of time: its hands were rigid, arrested mid-gesture. I read later that the mechanism had stopped at 10:17; the note was dry and precise, the sort of entry made when someone decides it is better to have a measurement than a sense. The clock's brass was bright at the edges and dull where dust had settled; nothing about it suggested violence, only interruption.

Between the fireplace and the only exterior window a wide desk took the light. Lena Harrow had been at that desk. She sat now with her upper body pitched forward as if in the middle of writing a sentence that never finished. One arm lay across the blotter; the other clutched a small square of linen whose corners were stained a dark, thirsty red. The hand under it had closed until the fabric puckered.

Set deep into Lena's chest was a heavy brass letter-opener — the blunt, workmanlike kind kept for opening estate envelopes rather than as ornament. It had been driven in with force enough to bend the ribs faintly around it. The haft carried no neat fingerprint to place an ordinary hand; there was, however, a thin smear of oil along the wood, the kind left by someone whose hands had been working on machinery rather than on paper. The smear caught the light at the edge, almost apologetic.

The window was the library's only break to the outside, a single-pane sash with a heavy latch that closed against the frame. On the outer sill, tucked into the ivy so it did not show unless you leaned, I found a short length of cord and a little loop of metal serving as a makeshift anchor. The housekeeper's note in the bag read that it was an improvised pulley anchor, hidden in the ivy; it looked exactly the sort of small, practical modification you make when you have a task to do and do not wish to be observed.

Milne kept returning, in his mind, to the bolt. "We lock it, we call it something neat," he said at one point, rubbing his jaw. He wanted a verdict on the case as if paper and procedure could smooth away questions. He spoke of drafting the file by teatime; his timetable was a pressure in the room.

I did not want neat. I wanted trouble. The misfits are the thing that opens a locked house: an oil smear where a hand should carry prints, a pulley anchored where no respectable customer would fit it, a handkerchief with a monogram that did not belong to the dead woman. The handkerchief's initials were not listed on the slip — they were simply noted as present — and that absence kept the name inside the cloth like a secret. Whoever had clenched it had made certain of being remembered, or of not being recognised at all.

It was small things that made me lean forward and look twice: the tack of polishing wax on the desk lip, the faint crescent of cigar ash on the sill that did not match Lena's habits, the particular way the clock's hands burned at 10:17 on a brass face now still. Milne saw disorder where I saw opportunity; he wanted to pin the scene with his bolt and leave. I wanted to find the thread that would unravel the neatness.

I ran a fingertip along the desk edge without touching where the opener had been, feeling for the ghost of oil under the varnish. Outside, the ivy moved with a dry, patient sound. Inside, a clock kept the exact wrong time. Milne asked if I had a theory. I told him not yet — that is the moment when an open case becomes one worth solving.

## The draft

I asked them to come back in the morning. Daylight makes liars smaller and mechanisms larger; Milne arrived with his notebook like a blunt instrument, Mary with her hands folded as if she might lay them over the truth, Oliver with his face the colour of peat, and Henry as composed as a man who expects a room to agree with him.

I set the window as I had the night before: a short loop of cord through the little metal eye in the ivy, the letter-opener lashed to it so the haft hung true. I placed a cloth against the sash to take the bite; I put the clock where the hands could no longer be trusted and told Milne to time me with his watch. They watched where people watch at trials — not at the instrument, but at the person who uses it.

My hands are better at small betrayals than at speeches. I threaded the cord through the loop again, felt the loop take the weight with a little give, and let the opener rest in my palm. The brass was cold; it filled my hand the way a small animal fills a glove. I thumbed the gap on the sash — a thumb's breadth, just enough; the glass yielded like skin. I pushed the opener through, feeling the resistance of the cloth as it closed about metal. The haft slipped, the oil on it catching the light like a dry promise.

There are sounds no one notices until you make them matter: the shush of cord through ivy, the faint drag as metal meets seal, the cloth's brief, surprised surrender. I drew the opener free, wound the cord a single, sure turn, and with a small pull the sash settled as if it had never been moved. Milne's watch ran the seconds out loud; when I let my fingers go he said the number into the air: "Less than a minute." It was the sort of shortness that unmakes alibis.

I did not let the demonstration speak for the whole case. I laid the things out on the desk: the folio with the ragged gap where a page had been torn cleanly away; the smear of oil that ran to the folio's edge and stopped; the handkerchief from Lena's palm, its corners blood-darkened. Under daylight the monogram was still smudged and unreadable — no tidy initials caught the eye. I did not pretend the cloth named him; its letters were, for all the room's clear light, illegible.

I placed the ashtray where it had been; the household recognised the brand by habit even if the laboratory had not stamped it for the file. The oil on the opener matched the smear by the folio in the way that a fingerprint matches a face: not absolute proof, but a joining of small things. Whoever could make the sash open from outside with a loop in the ivy and an obedient weight could thrust a blunt instrument through the gap and withdraw it without leaving the window visibly disturbed. Whoever could do that would know to smudge oil on the haft and on a page to make the trace look like toil rather than malice.

It was Henry who answered the chain I had laid. He had kept his face like a ledger's cover for too long. Milne asked the question I wanted him to: "Where were you between ten and half past?"

Henry's gloves came off in a small, quick gesture. "I went to her window," he said. The words came out flat, like a coin on a table. "I couldn't stand her tallying me — the things she had written. She loved that folio more than she loved me. I meant to go, to frighten her, to make her stop — I didn't think it would be like that." His hand shook, as if he had only just felt how heavy the opener had been.

Henry admitted, on the record, that he feared the ledger's entries about him and that fear had driven him to act. He told them how he'd fixed the loop in the ivy, knotted the cord, made the opener a weight and a blade for the same motion, and how he'd pulled the sash neat again. He admitted the torn page. "I took the sheet out. I could not have it in her book. It would have ruined me." In his words the quarrel over money and the will took a sharper shape: not only dispute, but dread of a ledger that would read him bankrupt in reputation.

Milne's notebook closed with a dull, practiced noise. He did not find the case tidy; he found it finished. He stepped forward when Henry's anger ran to a thin, legal thing and took him by the wrist. Mary said nothing at first; Oliver's hands were empty of tools but full of relief. I thought then of small proofs and larger truths: the demonstration had made the how visible; a man's admission had made the why indisputable.

Milne wanted neat words for the file. I wanted the sort of certainty that does not fit neatly on a form. I let him have the paperwork. For once, paper and blunt instruments agreed.
